Specifically, this SoK examines the security implications of Software-Defined Networking, Network Slicing, Separation Kernels, and Cross-Domain Solutions while addressing challenges posed by quantum computing through Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). This SoK provides a comprehensive analysis of the shift from hardware isolation to software segregation, serving as a crucial foundation for researchers and industry stakeholders aiming to enhance secure and adaptable VCS infrastructures for mission-critical operations.

9fe0e97c1dfab94e1a2321e2.title_original: Codetta: High-Capacity, Keyless, and Undetectable Multi-Agent Collusion
9fe0e97c1dfab94e1a2321e2.excerpt: arXiv:2609.28900v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings such as finance, healthcare, and software engineering, where agents coordinate through natural-language messages. The same channels, however, let colluding agents exfiltrate confidential information or coordinate unauthorized actions, and steganography can hide such communication inside outputs that look ordinary to an auditor reading the transcript. Existing provably undetectable LLM steganography protocols are not suited to realistic deployments. High-capacity schemes assume a symmetric setting where the receiver can reproduce the sender's output distribution, the state-of-the-art protocol for asymmetric agents has very low capacity, and most approaches rely on a pre-shared secret key. We make the threat of undetectable agent collusion concrete with Codetta, a high-capacity steganographic protocol for independently deployed agents in realistic asymmetric settings. Codetta combines a shared public model that estimates the communication channel, a sampling mechanism that preserves the sender's output distribution, and an adaptive error-correcting code. It further removes the pre-shared key through a steganographic key exchange that lets independently deployed agents establish a shared key while keeping the transcript computationally indistinguishable from ordinary model outputs. Across three agent workloads and three sender models, Codetta achieves up to $102\times$ the capacity of the state-of-the-art asymmetric protocol, and its key exchange establishes a shared key with about 80k visible tokens at an empirically certified failure probability of at most $4.1\times 10^{-3}$. These results show that effectively undetectable collusion is becoming feasible between independently deployed agents, so auditing must go beyond inspecting communication transcripts.

3b82177d466d3c76983b93c4.title_original: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
3b82177d466d3c76983b93c4.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24359v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together. The benchmark and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MemJoin-01BF/.

1bcf2322c6792107e777dbc1.title_original: ReDence: A Hybrid Agentic and System One Model Framework for Rapid, Evidence-Grounded Detection of Social Engineering Scams
1bcf2322c6792107e777dbc1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.30963v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Detecting online social engineering (SE) scams often requires examining website workflows, verifying claims against external sources, and connecting evidence across multiple pages. Existing detectors provide limited support for these tasks and rarely produce actionable evidence to support their decisions, leaving analysts to manually investigate flagged websites, which inevitably delays detection and subsequent takedown of these attacks. To address this gap, we present ReDence, a hybrid framework for automated, evidence-grounded scam investigation, detection, and reporting across diverse SE scam categories. ReDence combines two locally deployed, fine-tuned models: a multimodal agentic Investigator (Qwen3.5-4B) for investigative planning, evidence interpretation, and report generation, and a specialized System One model (Tev1) that handles binary and multiple-choice decisions, including browser action selection and evidence assessment, significantly reducing response generation overhead while preserving the Investigator's reasoning capabilities for complex tasks. The reports produced by ReDence also document investigative actions, collected evidence, and the reasoning behind each decision. Our evaluation shows that ReDence has a detection accuracy of over 96%, outperforming existing detectors while being at least four times faster. When deployed on a real-world URL stream over the period of 28 days, ReDence identified 4,042 new SE scam websites across 17 categories, of which at least 71% were missed by all four popular anti-scam blocklists evaluated. Feedback from twelve domain providers indicated that ReDence's investigative reports helped analysts recognize the scams documented in reported websites, understand the supporting evidence, and validate cases more efficiently. We open-source ReDence to aid automated, evidence-grounded scam investigation and reporting.

290f0804465ac4697602b91b.title_original: Permitted but Unauthorized: Affordance-Induced Delegated-Scope Violations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
290f0804465ac4697602b91b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.04086v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems place several agents on shared infrastructure, where each agent holds permissions far broader than the task it is delegated -- so every agent is routinely permitted to act on a peer's resources it was never assigned. We ask: under competitive pressure, what determines whether an agent crosses from its delegated scope into a peer's resources, and can such crossings be enforced away? We study this across eight LLMs in two simulated environments -- a CI/CD release pipeline and a security-operations incident queue -- using a deterministic, no-model-in-the-loop detector over hash-chained, replay-verified logs. In a controlled 2x2x2 factorial over competitive incentive, candidate visibility, and payoff information (three models, n=52 per cell), we find that action representation, not permission, governs the behavior: no agent crosses when the peer action is unlisted, whereas listing it under competitive pressure with a stated payoff raises crossings sharply -- up to 52 of 52 episodes for Claude Sonnet 4.5. We also observe a model-dependent split: two newer models (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5) refuse the identical attack in 0 of 100 episodes, where prior-generation models cross in 9 of 10. We then evaluate two defenses -- a deterministic reference monitor and a model-based pre-execution judge -- both block every crossing and, when the task is winnable, cut avoidable peer deadline misses from 15/40 and 14/40 to at most 1/40. But scope enforcement is not harm prevention: an agent can still set a peer back through an authorized action on its own resources -- misreporting its incident's severity -- which neither defense detects. Our results establish action representation, not permission alone, as a controllable driver of inter-agent scope violations, and show that enforcing delegated scope is distinct from preventing harm, motivating effect-aware authorization.

4aabae45e7eeb37c735e4334.title_original: A counterexample to the soundness of the Flowering IOPP for codes on graphs
4aabae45e7eeb37c735e4334.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21396v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Flowering protocol of Delavenne, Medevielle and Roussel (ISIT 2025, arXiv:2501.14337) and its generalization by Delavenne and Lallemand (CANS 2025, arXiv:2508.10510) are Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity (IOPPs) for codes on graphs with Reed-Solomon local codes. Similarly to FRI for Reed-Solomon codes, the graph is recursively cut into isomorphic subgraphs and the word is folded along the cuts. We show that the soundness claims of both papers are false. The commit soundness proofs identify the vertex distance of a word to the code with the fraction of its unsatisfied local constraints, while only one inequality holds, in the wrong direction. We furthermore give an explicit counterexample.

e9ec692233e818851d230ae0.title_original: A Forensic Analysis of Metadata and Information Leakage in Swedish Public Documents
e9ec692233e818851d230ae0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21922v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study investigates metadata and structural content leakage in publicly available PDF documents from 30 Swedish public-sector authorities. Using an automated collection pipeline and ExifTool-based extraction, 2,876 documents were analyzed and classified using an R0-R3 risk taxonomy. Results reveal that 48.4% of documents exhibit significant metadata exposure (R2 or R3), with significant variation across institutional tiers (p < 0.001). Longitudinal analysis across three legislative periods reveals a statistically significant reduction in metadata exposure between the baseline and post-enactment periods, yet 44.9% of documents published after the enactment of the Swedish Cybers\"akerhetslagen continue to leak sensitive metadata. Furthermore, 41.6% of documents contain incremental update layers; forensic analysis recovered verifiable text alterations, including deleted personal data and internal identifiers, from 228 of these cases. These findings highlight persistent regulatory lag and a systemic reliance on default, unsanitized document publication workflows within the Swedish public sector.

28cab3a6901527fd8eb56bc3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25509v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

e15fa933b2d655fcad34e285.title_original: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
e15fa933b2d655fcad34e285.excerpt: arXiv:2611.26298v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

421bbe20cf3c6855400a2f67.title_original: Hypercube LSH for approximate near neighbors
421bbe20cf3c6855400a2f67.excerpt: arXiv:1702.05760v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A celebrated technique for finding near neighbors for the angular distance involves using a set of random hyperplanes to partition the space into hash regions [Charikar, STOC 2002]. Experiments later showed that using a set of orthogonal hyperplanes, thereby partitioning the space into the Voronoi regions induced by a hypercube, leads to even better results [Terasawa and Tanaka, WADS 2007]. However, no theoretical explanation for this improvement was ever given, and it remained unclear how the resulting hypercube hash method scales in high dimensions. In this work, we provide explicit asymptotics for the collision probabilities when using hypercubes to partition the space. Vectors at angle $\pi/3$ collide with probability $(\sqrt{3}/\pi)^{d + o(d)}$ in dimension $d$, compared to $(2/3)^d$ for random hyperplanes, and near-parallel vectors collide with similar asymptotic probabilities in both cases. The limiting exponential base tends continuously to zero as the angle approaches $\frac{\pi}{2}$ from below. For fixed near and far angular thresholds below $\pi/2$, these asymptotics determine the limiting LSH collision-probability ratio $\rho$. We further describe how to use hypercube LSH in practice. A direct partial-hypercube analysis gives a heuristic lattice-sieving time bound $2^{0.3347d+o(d)}$.

a9779acb1980062a6cb37f57.excerpt: arXiv:2604.00942v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern data analysis increasingly relies on manifold-based methods that use local geometry to extract low-dimensional structure from noisy observations. Yet in domains such as biomedicine and public health, privacy regulations restrict access to individual-level data, while perturbations introduced to protect privacy can distort the geometric information needed for analysis. We introduce a manifold denoising framework that uses private reference data to correct noisy public queries, bringing differential privacy to local geometric estimation. Starting from a hard correction based on the estimated tangent space, we develop a noise-adaptive soft correction that avoids specifying the intrinsic dimension. Furthermore, we construct a shared Gaussian field that couples evaluations across locations and bandwidths with moderate marginal noise inflation. Under standard assumptions on manifold regularity and sampling density, we establish non-asymptotic utility guarantees that characterize how denoising accuracy depends on sample size, noise level, bandwidth, and the privacy budget. Simulations and UK Biobank applications demonstrate accurate signal recovery under moderate privacy budgets. These results illustrate clear utility--privacy trade-offs and provide a practical DP component for manifold-based workflows in regulated environments.

75485d8523ee8a6c77d1d864.title_original: Supply Chain Compromise Backdoors Six WP connect Plugins, Blocked by WordPress.org’s Release Hold
75485d8523ee8a6c77d1d864.excerpt: On November 22nd, 2026, a threat actor pushed backdoored releases of six WordPress plugins developed by WP connect, including Air WP Sync, WP Sync for Notion, and Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms, which together are estimated to have more than 3,600 active installations. Each release silently loaded the same remote-control module, which phones home to an attacker-controlled server, executes any PHP code it is sent, and exposes a full command set for running shell commands, stealing password hashes, and planting webshells. Thanks to safeguards introduced under WordPress.org’s Protect The Shire initiative, the backdoored versions were never released to sites, and all six plugins were closed on WordPress.org the same evening. While the WordPress plugins team independently detected and stopped this threat, Wordfence’s PRISM also discovered and notified our team to the threat, which was then validated by our team. As a reminder, PRISM is our continuous monitoring and vulnerability research agent created by the Wordfence Threat Intelligence team. The backdoor in Air WP Sync was also independently discovered and reported by Computeronfire , and we thank them for their contribution. Our mission is to secure WordPress through defense in depth, which is why we are investing in proactive vulnerability research of this kind alongside our Bug Bounty Program . We are committed to making the WordPress ecosystem more secure through the detection and prevention of vulnerabilities, which is a critical element to our multi-layered approach to security. While no sites should have a backdoored copy of these plugins, out of an abundance of caution we are developing malware signatures to detect the backdoor, which will be released to Wordfence Premium , Wordfence Care , and Wordfence Response users first. Because the malicious versions were never released, most sites running these plugins should not be affected. However, it is still important to verify that your site is not running one of the compromised versions listed below. Unlike a typical vulnerability, this was not a coding mistake, and there is no patch: the malicious code was added deliberately and committed to each plugin’s WordPress.org repository. The affected plugins remain closed on WordPress.org at the time of this publication. The affected releases unconditionally load a backdoor module (includes/airwp-online.php) that runs on every request via the 'init' hook and on a half-hourly WP-Cron event, sends site information (site URL, PHP, WordPress and OS versions, and the server user) to a remote command-and-control server at tascredit-pay.com with TLS certificate verification disabled, and executes the PHP code returned by that server via eval(). The module also accepts queued commands that run shell commands, read, write and delete arbitrary files, query arbitrary database tables, dump the users table including password hashes, drop a webshell into the uploads directory, and install persistent hourly code execution. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers in control of the remote server, or able to intercept its traffic, to execute arbitrary code on the server and fully compromise affected sites. All affected plugins have been closed on WordPress.org and no patched versions are available; we strongly recommend uninstalling them and running a complete malware scan. 2efe3b69edf2d45a1098be62.title_original: Staying Ahead of the New Threat Landscape in 2027
2efe3b69edf2d45a1098be62.excerpt: The WordPress threat landscape changed drastically in 2026, and we expect the pace to continue in 2027. Security researchers are using AI coding agents to find vulnerabilities faster. So are attackers. In response, we built our own AI research systems, Wordfence PRISM and Wordfence Argus , which are credited with more than 500 published vulnerability discoveries, and invested heavily in the models, analysts and processes that turn those discoveries into protection for over 5 million WordPress sites. Below, we share the details of that work and how we’re investing in staying ahead of threats in 2027. How the WordPress Threat Landscape Changed in 2026 This year brought the first critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in WordPress core in nearly a decade and two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the language WordPress runs on . AI coding agents have developed rapidly over the past year, and they quickly surpassed what was humanly capable in vulnerability research. Finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in code used to take years of expertise and significant effort to understand and carry out. Now researchers increasingly do that work with AI coding tools and agentic security testing harnesses. In April, we reported that AI-assisted reports had grown from 16% to roughly 66% of submissions to our Bug Bounty Program . So far in November, 88% of the reports independent researchers have submitted to the program are AI-assisted. The same tools are available to attackers, and they are already using them. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group recently described an attacker framework that monitors popular web software for security patches, compares the code before and after each fix to find the vulnerability, writes an exploit and runs it without any human involvement. One of the examples Google published shows the framework analyzing a WordPress plugin. Tools like this shorten the time between a patch being released and attackers exploiting it, so how quickly protection reaches a site matters more than it used to. At Wordfence, our mission is to secure the web. In 2026, that meant building our own AI research tools and investing heavily in the most capable security research models we could access, including some that are not publicly available and are offered only to approved security teams. Finding Vulnerabilities Before Attackers Do Wordfence PRISM , our AI vulnerability research system, is credited with 504 published vulnerability discoveries as of November 23, 296 of them in the last 90 days. In the past 30 days alone it was credited with 149 findings, across more than 100 different plugins and themes. Wordfence Argus , our autonomous research agent, is credited with 17 published discoveries since late August, 16 of them rated High or Critical. They include a six-step critical remote code execution chain in the Avada theme , two unauthenticated remote code execution chains in The Events Calendar , and an unauthenticated file upload vulnerability in Gravity Forms . Argus also found critical vulnerabilities beyond WordPress, in libheif and Ghostscript , system software that many servers, media tools and document pipelines rely on to process images and PDFs. Every vulnerability our AI systems report is reviewed by a Wordfence analyst before it is published or sent to a vendor. Our own research runs alongside the work of independent researchers in our Bug Bounty Program , which has paid more than $1 million in bounties since it launched, including more than $436,000 awarded so far this year, up from $259,000 in all of 2025. The work of independent researchers remains essential, because the more people and tools looking at WordPress software, the fewer vulnerabilities are left for attackers to find first. Turning Discoveries Into Protection More reports also mean more to sort through. Of the more than 16,700 reports submitted to us in 2026, about 4,400 were confirmed as valid vulnerabilities, and most of the rest were duplicates or did not hold up. To keep pace, our Threat Intelligence team uses a multi-agent AI pipeline that checks each submitted report against the real software before it reaches an analyst, so our analysts spend their time on confirmed vulnerabilities and valid reports reach vendors and our firewall team faster. From there, we work with WordPress plugin and theme vendors to get vulnerabilities patched as soon as possible. More than 1,000 vendors have registered for our Vulnerability Management Portal, covering more than 5,000 plugins and themes. The portal streamlines disclosure, so vendors receive reports quickly and patches reach site owners sooner. In the meantime, we deploy firewall rules and malware signatures through the Wordfence plugin. Wordfence Premium, Care, and Response customers receive them in real time. Real-time protection matters most for software that does not update on its own. Many premium plugins and themes are not distributed through WordPress.org and often do not update automatically, so a firewall rule can be the only thing protecting a site until its owner updates manually. We also screen new plugin versions for malicious code, such as backdoors added through a compromised developer account. In July, PRISM detected a backdoored WordPress plugin less than two hours after the malicious code was introduced , and this month it flagged a supply chain compromise of six WP connect plugins , which WordPress.org’s release hold stopped before the backdoored versions reached any sites. Catching a malicious update early means it can be flagged before it spreads to the sites that install it. We also publish the research for free on Wordfence Intelligence , along with a vulnerability data feed API and webhook notifications , which practitioners and larger security platforms rely on for threat data.
